column2:
You are standing up an insurance claims-processing pipeline on Amazon Bedrock in us-east-1. Two failures appear on the first day of testing: every converse call that names the Claude model by its base model ID fails with an error that the model is not available in the region, and every call to the Titan Text Embeddings model fails with an error that your account does not have access to that model. Calls to both models from a teammate's account in another region succeed.

Which TWO changes resolve these failures? (Select TWO.)

A. Wrap both calls in a retry with exponential backoff, since the errors indicate transient capacity problems in the region.
B. Replace the base model ID with the model's cross-region inference profile ID so Bedrock routes the request to a region that hosts the model.
C. Switch from converse to invoke_model, which accepts models that are not yet enabled or hosted in the region.
D. Request access to the Titan embeddings model on the Bedrock console's model access page for your account.
column3:
Correct Answer: B and D. Option B addresses the first failure: not every model is hosted in every region, and a base model ID sent to a region that lacks the model produces exactly this error; an inference profile ID (found under cross-region inference rather than the model catalog) lets Bedrock route the request to a region where the model actually runs. Option D addresses the second failure: access to a foundation model must be enabled per account in the Bedrock console before it can be invoked, which is why the same model works from a teammate's account. Option A treats deterministic configuration errors as transient and would retry forever. Option C changes the invocation API, but model hosting and model access are enforced identically for invoke_model.

Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration)

References:
• Cross-region inference (AWS docs)
• Bedrock model access (AWS docs)
• Claude on Amazon Bedrock

column2:
A developer on your financial-services document intake team ports a helper from a prior project that used the Anthropic Python SDK. On Bedrock the helper's client.converse(...) call succeeds, but reading the generated text with response["content"][0]["text"] raises a KeyError on every request.

What is the correct way to read the generated text from the Converse response?

A. json.loads(response["body"].read())["content"][0]["text"], since Bedrock returns a streaming body that must be decoded first.
B. response["completion"], which Converse populates with the concatenated text of all parts.
C. response["content"][0]["text"] after adding anthropic_version to the request, which switches Converse to the Anthropic response format.
D. response["output"]["message"]["content"][0]["text"], because Converse wraps the assistant message in an output envelope.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: the Converse API returns an envelope in which the assistant message lives under output and then message, and the message's content is a list of parts, so the first text part is at response["output"]["message"]["content"][0]["text"]. The Bedrock API and the Anthropic API are different services with different SDKs and response shapes, which is why the ported path fails. Option A describes reading an invoke_model response body, not a Converse response. Option B names a field Converse does not return. Option C mixes the two APIs; anthropic_version belongs in the native invoke_model request body and does not change Converse's envelope.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration)

References:
• Converse API (AWS docs)
• Claude on Amazon Bedrock
• Anthropic Claude Messages API on Bedrock (AWS docs)

column2:
Your team copies a request from the Anthropic Messages API documentation into a boto3 converse call for a healthcare intake assistant, passing system="You are an intake assistant..." as a plain string and temperature=0.2 as a top-level keyword argument. boto3 rejects the call with a parameter validation error before any request leaves the machine.

What is the most direct fix?

A. Move both values into additionalModelRequestFields, since they are Anthropic-specific parameters that Converse passes through untouched.
B. Switch to invoke_model with an anthropic_version body, because Converse does not support system prompts.
C. Pass the system prompt as system=[{"text": "..."}] and the temperature inside inferenceConfig={"temperature": 0.2}, following the Converse request shape.
D. Set the client's region to one that hosts the model; the validation error is a symptom of cross-region routing.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. The Converse API defines its own request shape: the system prompt is a list of content parts ([{"text": ...}]), and sampling settings such as temperature and stop sequences live inside inferenceConfig. Requests written against the Anthropic API's shape fail boto3's client-side validation because the two services use different SDKs and parameter names. Option A misuses additionalModelRequestFields, which exists for model-specific fields that Converse does not model natively, not for standard fields it already defines. Option B is wrong on the facts: Converse supports system prompts, and invoke_model would require rewriting the entire request body. Option D addresses a routing problem, but this error is raised locally before any request reaches a region.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration)

References:
• Converse API (AWS docs)
• Anthropic Claude Messages API on Bedrock (AWS docs)
• Claude on Amazon Bedrock

column2:
Your financial-services intake service builds each request by appending a user message containing the full text of a 30-page filing and then appending a second user message containing the analyst's question. Every call fails with a validation error stating that conversation roles must alternate between user and assistant.

How should the request be restructured?

A. Send the filing and the question as two text parts inside the content list of a single user message.
B. Insert a placeholder assistant message such as Understood. between the two user messages so the roles alternate.
C. Send the filing in one converse call, then send the question in a second call, relying on Bedrock to retain the first.
D. Move the filing text into the system parameter as a string and keep the question as the only user message.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: a message's content is a list precisely so that one message can carry several parts (multiple text parts, or text alongside documents or images). Placing the filing and the question as two parts of one user message satisfies the user-then-assistant alternation rule while keeping both in the same turn. Option B fabricates an assistant turn that Claude never produced, which distorts the conversation and is an unreliable workaround. Option C fails because Bedrock is stateless and stores nothing between calls; the second request would contain no filing. Option D misuses the system prompt, which must itself be a list of text parts, for per-request document content.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration)

References:
• Converse API (AWS docs)
• Working with messages

column2:
A new engineer on your claims pipeline creates the client with boto3.client("bedrock", region_name="us-west-2"). Calls that list the available foundation models work, but client.converse(...) raises AttributeError: 'Bedrock' object has no attribute 'converse'.

What is the cause?

A. The installed boto3 version predates Converse; upgrading boto3 adds the converse method to the bedrock client.
B. Converse must be enabled per model in the Bedrock console before the method appears on the client.
C. The us-west-2 region does not support Converse, so boto3 omits the method for clients created there.
D. The converse operation lives on the bedrock-runtime client, which invokes models; the bedrock client is the control-plane API.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. Bedrock exposes two boto3 clients: bedrock is the control plane (listing models, managing access and jobs), while bedrock-runtime is the data plane that actually invokes models through converse, converse_stream, and invoke_model. The course's request setup connects to the Bedrock runtime for exactly this reason. Option A is wrong because the method never lives on the control-plane client regardless of version. Option B confuses model access enablement, which produces an access error at call time, with a missing SDK method. Option C is wrong because boto3 builds client methods from the service definition, not from regional support.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration)

References:
• Converse API (AWS docs)
• What is Amazon Bedrock (AWS docs)
• Claude on Amazon Bedrock

column2:
Your shared chat() helper for the healthcare intake assistant always passes system=[{"text": system_prompt}] to converse. Callers that have no system prompt pass an empty string, and 100% of those calls fail with a validation error that the system prompt must contain at least one character.

What is the most appropriate change to the helper?

A. Default the system prompt to a single space so the parameter is never empty and validation always passes.
B. Build the request parameters as a dictionary and add the system key only when a non-empty prompt is supplied.
C. Move the callers' instructions into the first user message and remove the system parameter entirely.
D. Wrap the call in a retry that strips the system parameter after the first validation failure.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: Bedrock requires that a system prompt, if present, contain at least one character, so the clean design is a helper whose system prompt defaults to None and that includes the system key in the converse parameters only when a prompt is provided. Option A sends a meaningless one-character prompt on every call just to satisfy validation. Option C removes the system prompt for everyone, discarding the role-based control that callers who do supply a prompt rely on. Option D turns a known, deterministic validation rule into a failed request plus a retry on every call.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration)

References:
• Converse API (AWS docs)
• System prompts (role prompting)

column2:
Your claims-processing agent on Bedrock calls a lookup_policy tool. When the policy service throws, the handler catches the exception and returns a toolResult block with "is_error": true and the exception text, a pattern copied from the Anthropic API. boto3 rejects these follow-up requests with a parameter validation error on the tool result block.

How should the handler signal the failure on Bedrock?

A. Raise the exception out of the handler so the agent loop stops and the error is logged for an engineer.
B. Return "status": "success" with an empty content list so Claude infers that the lookup found nothing.
C. Set "status": "error" on the toolResult block and put the error message in its content list.
D. Put the error text in a separate text part of the user message and omit the toolResult block.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: in the Converse API a toolResult block carries a status field whose value is success or error, with the error details supplied as text in content; there is no is_error field, so the Anthropic-API spelling fails validation. Returning an error status lets Claude read the message and often retry with corrected arguments. Option A terminates the whole conversation for a recoverable tool failure. Option B disguises a failure as an empty success, so Claude confidently reports that no policy exists. Option D leaves the toolUse block without a matching toolResult, which is itself a validation error, and strips the error of its association with the call.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.3

References:

• Handle tool calls
• Troubleshooting tool use

column2:
Your intake assistant's loop sends the initial request with a toolConfig containing three toolSpec definitions. After executing the requested tool it appends the assistant message and a user message holding the toolResult, then calls converse again with only modelId and messages. The second call fails 100% of the time with a validation error referencing the toolUse and toolResult content blocks.

What is the fix?

A. Strip the toolUse and toolResult blocks from history before the follow-up call so the request contains only text.
B. Move the tool results into the system parameter so they are not counted as content blocks.
C. Replace the tool definitions with a note in the user message listing the tool names Claude already used.
D. Pass the same toolConfig on every call in the loop, since messages containing tool blocks require the tool definitions to be present.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: Converse requires toolConfig whenever the conversation contains toolUse or toolResult blocks, and Claude also needs the schemas to interpret the results it asked for, so the identical tool definitions must accompany every call in the loop, not just the first. Option A discards the tool call and result that the follow-up response depends on. Option B misuses the system prompt and breaks the pairing between a toolResult and its toolUseId. Option C describes tools in prose, which neither satisfies the API requirement nor gives Claude the schemas.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.3

References:
• Tool use on Bedrock (AWS docs)
• How tool use works

column2:
For the extraction step of your financial-services pipeline you want Claude to always call the extract_filing tool. Following an Anthropic API example, you set "toolChoice": {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_filing"} inside toolConfig, and boto3 rejects the request during parameter validation.

Which toolChoice value is correct for the Converse API?

A. {"any": {"name": "extract_filing"}}
B. {"tool": {"name": "extract_filing"}}
C. {"forced": {"tool": "extract_filing"}}
D. {"toolChoice": "extract_filing"}
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: in Converse, toolChoice is an object keyed by mode, where {"auto": {}} lets Claude decide, {"any": {}} requires some tool, and {"tool": {"name": ...}} forces a specific tool, whereas the Anthropic API uses a type discriminator. Option A misuses the any mode, which takes an empty object and cannot name a tool, so even if accepted it would not guarantee extract_filing. Options C and D are not valid Converse shapes at all.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.1

References:
• Tool use on Bedrock (AWS docs)
• Implement tool use

column2:
You are defining the get_claim_status tool for a Bedrock-based claims agent. Your first attempt places {"name": ..., "description": ..., "input_schema": {...}} directly in toolConfig.tools, and the request fails validation.

How must each tool be declared in toolConfig?

A. As a toolSpec object with name, description, and an inputSchema whose JSON Schema sits under a json key.
B. As a function object with name, description, and parameters, matching the declaration style used by other providers.
C. As a bare JSON Schema object whose title is used as the tool name and whose description doubles as the tool description.
D. As a toolSpec object with name and description only; the argument schema is inferred from the tool's first use.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: Converse wraps each tool in {"toolSpec": {"name": ..., "description": ..., "inputSchema": {"json": {...}}}}; the json wrapper and the camel-cased inputSchema are the Bedrock spelling of what the Anthropic API calls input_schema. Option B is another provider's format. Option C omits the explicit name and description that Claude relies on to choose and call the tool correctly. Option D is wrong because Claude never infers argument structure; the schema is what tells it which arguments to supply and with what types.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.1

References:
• Tool use on Bedrock (AWS docs)
• Define tools (schemas, descriptions)

column2:
To cut sequential round trips, your claims agent on Bedrock adds a batch_tool whose toolSpec takes an invocations list, each entry holding a tool name and its arguments as a JSON-encoded string. The first test crashes with TypeError: argument after ** must be a mapping, and after that is patched Bedrock rejects the follow-up because the handler returned three toolResult blocks for the single batch_tool call.

Which TWO changes make the handler work? (Select TWO.)

A. Parse each invocation's arguments with json.loads before dispatching it through the existing run_tool function.
B. Set toolChoice to the batch tool on every request so Claude always groups its calls into one invocation list.
C. Rewrite the assistant message so that each invocation appears as its own toolUse block before sending the results.
D. Collect the outputs of all invocations into one list and return them as a single toolResult bearing the batch call's toolUseId.
column3:
Correct Answer: A and D. Option A fixes the crash: the batch spec encodes arguments as a JSON string, so the handler must decode it into a dictionary before splatting it into the target tool, and delegating to the existing dispatcher keeps one implementation per tool. Option D fixes the rejection: from Bedrock's perspective there was exactly one toolUse (the batch call), so exactly one toolResult with its toolUseId must come back, containing the combined outputs. Option B forces the batch tool even for single-tool or no-tool turns and does nothing about the handler defects. Option C tampers with the model's own message, breaking the pairing between the real toolUse and its result.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.3

References:
• Tool use on Bedrock (AWS docs)
• Parallel tool use
• Handle tool calls

column2:
Your healthcare intake assistant's chat() helper returns content[0]["text"] from every Converse response. Once tools were enabled, 9% of turns raise a KeyError; the logs show those responses begin with a toolUse part, and other turns silently lose text that appeared after the first part.

How should the helper extract the reply text?

A. Keep index 0 but wrap it in a try/except that returns an empty string whenever the first part has no text key.
B. Instruct Claude in the system prompt to always begin its reply with a text part before any tool call.
C. Collect the text values from every part that has a text key and join them, leaving tool parts to the tool handler.
D. Set toolChoice to {"auto": {}} on every request so that responses are guaranteed to start with a text part.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: a Converse assistant message's content is a list of parts that may hold text, toolUse, and other part types in any order, so the helper should gather all text parts rather than assume position 0 is text. Option A hides the problem and returns nothing on the very turns where Claude included a tool call plus text. Option B relies on prompt compliance for a structural guarantee the API does not make. Option D is already the default and does not control part ordering.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.3

References:
• Converse API (AWS docs)
• Handle tool calls
• Working with messages

column2:
You add the built-in text editor tool to a Bedrock-based code-fixing agent by passing the exact tool name for your Claude version in additionalModelRequestFields. Claude responds with toolUse parts such as {"command": "view", "path": "./handler.py"} and later str_replace, but no files are read or changed, and the run ends with Claude asking you for the file contents.

What is missing?

A. A toolSpec for the text editor inside toolConfig, since passing the built-in name alone does not register the tool's schema with Claude.
B. File contents embedded in the system prompt, because the text editor tool can only operate on text that is already in context.
C. A switch to an MCP filesystem server, since the built-in text editor tool is read-only when used through Bedrock.
D. Your own handlers for each editor command (view, str_replace, create, insert) that perform the file operation and return a toolResult.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: for the text editor tool, only the tool's schema is built into Claude; the developer must implement a handler for each command that actually touches the file system and send each outcome back as a toolResult. Without them, Claude's toolUse requests go unanswered, which is why it ends up asking for the file contents. Option A is wrong because the built-in tool is enabled by name through the model request fields, not by a hand-written toolSpec. Option B misunderstands the tool, whose purpose is to let Claude read and edit files it does not yet have in context. Option C is unnecessary and factually off; the tool supports edits as soon as the handlers exist.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.1

References:
• Text editor tool
• Tool use on Bedrock (AWS docs)

column2:
In your claims agent the toolSpec names a tool get_current_datetime, while the dispatcher's run_tool function matches on the string get_current_date. Every attempt to use the tool raises the dispatcher's Unknown tool exception, and the model never 'corrects' the name no matter how the prompt is worded.

What is the root cause, and what is the fix?

A. Claude paraphrases tool names when prompts are informal; add the alternate spelling to the tool description so it learns the dispatcher's name.
B. The dispatcher must match the toolSpec name exactly, since Claude emits the schema's name verbatim; fix the typo in the dispatcher.
C. Bedrock normalizes tool names by dropping trailing words such as time; register the tool under the shortened name instead.
D. Return an error toolResult for the unknown name so Claude retries with the spelling the dispatcher expects.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: the name in a toolUse part is always the exact string declared in the toolSpec, so a mismatch between schema and dispatcher is a developer typo, and the dispatcher's key must be corrected to match the schema. Option A asks the model to work around your bug and is impossible anyway, since Claude can only call declared names. Option C invents behavior that Bedrock does not have. Option D cannot succeed because the only name Claude knows is the declared one; the loop would simply repeat the error.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.1

References:

• Troubleshooting tool use
• Tool use on Bedrock (AWS docs)

column2:
Your underwriting team extracts policy_number, date_of_loss, claim_amount, and claimant from claims letters on Bedrock. Today the pipeline asks for JSON in the reply text and parses it, which fails on 4% of letters; a teammate proposes switching to the flexible toJSON catch-all tool instead. The extracted values feed payment decisions.

Which TWO design choices best fit this pipeline? (Select TWO.)

A. Keep the prompt-based JSON approach but add a code-block prefill and a stop sequence so that the reply text parses reliably.
B. Define a dedicated toolSpec whose inputSchema mirrors the four fields and read them from the returned toolUse input.
C. Prefer the dedicated schema over the flexible toJSON tool for this task, reserving the flexible tool for lower-stakes extractions.
D. Adopt the flexible toJSON tool as proposed, since its open input schema adapts to unusual letter layouts without schema edits.
column3:
Correct Answer: B and C. Option B replaces text parsing with tool-based extraction: Claude 'calls' a tool whose inputs are the desired structure, so the fields arrive as schema-conformant arguments rather than free text that must be parsed. Option C applies the course's guidance on the two tool-based styles: the flexible toJSON tool is convenient for rapidly changing or low-stakes structures but yields somewhat lower-quality results, so a critical financial extraction warrants a dedicated schema. Option A keeps the fragile text-parsing path; a prefill and stop sequence make the JSON easier to locate but do not provide the schema-conformant arguments that a tool call does. Option D is the teammate's proposal: the flexible tool trades fidelity for convenience, which is the wrong trade when the values feed payment decisions.

References:

• Implement tool use
• anthropics/courses (GitHub)

column2:
Your document intake system extracts a different set of fields for each of 14 internal form types, and the field lists change monthly. The team maintains 14 hand-written toolSpec schemas and estimates 6 hours of schema edits per change cycle; none of the 14 outputs is used for regulated decisions.

Which approach best reduces maintenance while keeping extraction reliable?

A. Register one flexible toJSON tool with an open object input and specify each form type's properties and types in the prompt text.
B. Merge the 14 schemas into a single toolSpec with every possible field marked optional so one schema covers all forms.
C. Add a routing classifier that inspects each document and selects which of the 14 toolSpec schemas to send.
D. Return to prompt-based JSON extraction with a code-block prefill and stop sequence so that no schemas are needed at all.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is the course's flexible extraction pattern: a single toJSON tool whose input accepts arbitrary properties, with the desired structure written in the prompt, so changing a form's fields means editing prompt text rather than a schema. The trade-off is slightly lower fidelity than a dedicated schema, which is acceptable here because no output drives regulated decisions. Option B produces a sprawling schema in which Claude must guess which of dozens of optional fields apply to each form. Option C adds a classifier to solve a maintenance problem and still leaves 14 schemas to maintain. Option D gives up the reliability of tool-based extraction entirely.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3

References:
• Define tools (schemas, descriptions)
• anthropics/courses (GitHub)

column2:
Using the flexible toJSON tool, your claims pipeline extracts adjuster_name from intake emails. 18% of emails name no adjuster; in those cases Claude sometimes omits the key, sometimes returns an empty string, and in 3% of cases supplies a name found elsewhere in the email signature. Downstream code treats any string as a valid assignment.

What is the most effective change?

A. Mark adjuster_name as required in the toJSON tool's inputSchema so that Claude must always supply a value for it on every email.
B. Lower the temperature to 0 so that the behavior for emails with no adjuster becomes consistent and repeatable from run to run.
C. Run a second extraction call for each email and accept the adjuster name only when both calls agree.
D. State in the prompt's structure listing that adjuster_name must be null when no adjuster is named, and route null to manual assignment in code.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: with the flexible tool the schema is deliberately open, so the rules for each property, including what to do when the source lacks it, live in the prompt's structure listing; an explicit null convention gives downstream code an unambiguous signal instead of an absent key, an empty string, or a fabricated name. Option A cannot express the absent case; requiring the field pushes Claude toward inventing a value. Option B makes the output more repeatable but does not define what the correct output is. Option C doubles cost and still has no rule for the missing case, so both calls can agree on the same fabricated name.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3

References:
• Define tools (schemas, descriptions)
• Be clear and direct
• anthropics/courses (GitHub)

column2:
After switching your filing extractor to a forced extract_filing tool on Bedrock, the post-processing step calls json.loads(part["toolUse"]["input"]) and every run fails with TypeError: the JSON object must be str, bytes or bytearray, not dict.

What should the pipeline do with the tool input?

A. Call json.dumps on the input first so that json.loads can re-parse it into a clean dictionary.
B. Switch back to prompt-based extraction, since tool inputs cannot be read as JSON on Bedrock.
C. Use part["toolUse"]["input"] directly, because Converse delivers the tool arguments as an already-parsed dictionary.
D. Retry the request with a higher maxTokens so that the JSON arrives complete and can be parsed.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: in a Converse response the toolUse part's input is already a dictionary matching the tool's inputSchema, so the extracted values can be used as-is; the pipeline's parse step is redundant and is exactly what fails. Option A round-trips the data through a string for no reason. Option B abandons the more reliable extraction path over a misunderstanding of the response shape. Option D addresses truncation, which is not occurring; the error is a client-side type error.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3

References:
• Tool use on Bedrock (AWS docs)
• Handle tool calls

column2:
Your nightly Bedrock job extracts fields from about 9,000 claims letters. When extraction of any single letter fails validation (a missing required field or an unparseable date), the job raises and the entire run stops; on 3 of the last 5 nights, one bad letter delayed all 9,000 by a day.

How should the job handle a failed extraction?

A. Suppress validation errors and write whatever was extracted for that letter so that the run always completes on schedule.
B. Retry the failing letter up to five times with backoff and stop the run only if every retry fails.
C. Record the failure with the letter ID, failing field, and reason, route that letter to a review queue, and continue with the rest.
D. Wrap the whole batch in a single database transaction so that any failure rolls back every letter for consistency.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: one document's failure is an independent, recoverable event, so the job should capture structured error context (which letter, which field, why) that a reviewer can act on and keep processing the other letters. Option A silently passes unvalidated data into downstream systems. Option B still halts the run for a letter that may be genuinely unextractable, and blind retries of a deterministic validation failure rarely help. Option D maximizes the blast radius of a single failure, which is the current problem.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3

References:
• Troubleshooting tool use
• Handle tool calls

column2:
Claims arrive as PDFs. Your pipeline runs a separate OCR service, then sends the recovered text to Claude on Bedrock with a forced extraction tool. OCR errors account for 7% of wrong field values, and the OCR step adds 40 seconds per document.

What is the most direct simplification?

A. Keep the OCR step but add few-shot examples of common OCR misreads to the extraction prompt so Claude corrects them.
B. Send the PDF bytes as a document part (format pdf, name without extension) in the same user message as the instruction, and remove the OCR step.
C. Convert each PDF page to an image and send up to 20 image parts per request for Claude to transcribe before extracting.
D. Add a second Claude call that cleans the OCR output before the extraction call sees it.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: Claude on Bedrock reads PDF content directly when the file is supplied as a document content part alongside the text prompt, which removes the OCR service and its errors from the pipeline in one change. Option A keeps the flawed step and tries to prompt around its output. Option C reintroduces a conversion step and treats the PDF as a stack of images when native document input exists. Option D adds a second model call to clean up a step that can simply be removed.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3

References:
• PDF support
• Converse API (AWS docs)

column2:
Your insurance knowledge base uses hybrid retrieval (a vector index plus a BM25 index, merged with rank fusion). An audit of 400 adjuster questions shows the correct section is retrieved in 91% of cases but ranks second or third in 35% of them, and the prompt budget allows only the top result to be included.

Which change most directly improves the rank of the correct section?

A. Add a reranking step that sends the merged candidates to Claude with the query and reorders them by relevance before the prompt is built.
B. Increase the retrieval depth so that the top ten candidates are all placed in the prompt for the answer step to sort out.
C. Re-chunk the corpus with a larger overlap so that neighboring sections share more text and rank closer together.
D. Replace the embedding model with one that produces larger vectors and re-embed the entire corpus.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: the failure is ordering among already-retrieved candidates, which is exactly what an LLM reranker fixes: a post-processing call that reads the query and each candidate and returns them in decreasing relevance, at the cost of one extra model call's latency. Option B violates the stated prompt budget and pushes the ranking problem onto the answer step. Option C changes what is retrieved, not how candidates are ordered, and recall is already 91%. Option D is a speculative, expensive change with no evidence that embedding quality is the bottleneck.

Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.4

References:
• Contextual retrieval (Anthropic)
• Embeddings guidance
• anthropics/courses (GitHub)

column2:
After adding a Claude reranker to your claims knowledge base, answer accuracy rose from 78% to 90%, but p50 latency grew by 4 seconds. Profiling shows the reranker receives all 40 merged candidates and is asked to return the reordered chunks' full text, which averages 3,000 output tokens per query.

Which TWO changes cut the reranking latency while preserving most of the accuracy gain? (Select TWO.)

A. Assign a short temporary ID to each candidate and ask the reranker to return only the ordered IDs, mapping back to text in code.
B. Skip the reranker whenever the top two rank-fusion scores differ by more than 0.1, since the leader is then clear.
C. Rerank only the top 10 merged candidates instead of all 40.
D. Drop the BM25 index so that fewer candidates are produced for the reranker to read.
column3:
Correct Answer: A and C. Option A removes the dominant cost: having Claude copy chunk text back is slow and wasteful, whereas returning an ordered list of IDs takes a handful of tokens and lets code look up the text. Option C shrinks the reranker's input to the candidates that could plausibly be top-ranked, cutting input tokens without discarding the ordering benefit. Option B uses a score gap as a confidence proxy, but rank-fusion scores are coarse and the failures reranking fixes are precisely the cases where a wrong candidate leads; it silently skips the fix. Option D reduces recall for exact-term queries to save a small amount of reranker input.

column2:
Your financial-services research assistant chunks 80-page reports by section. Chunks refer to 'the incident' or 'the program' without naming them, since the names appear only in each report's introduction. Queries that name the incident retrieve the introduction but miss the sections that actually discuss it; recall on such queries is 58%.

Which change best addresses the failure?

A. Add a reranking step so that the sections discussing the incident move above the introduction in the merged results list.
B. Increase chunk overlap so that each section includes the tail of the previous section and inherits some of its wording.
C. Add few-shot examples to the answer prompt showing how to interpret unnamed references such as 'the incident' or 'the program'.
D. Before indexing, have Claude write a short context situating each chunk within the full report, prepend it, and index the contextualized chunk.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is contextual retrieval: chunking strips each section of document-level context, and a preprocessing step that asks Claude to situate the chunk within the source document restores references such as the incident's name into the text that gets embedded and indexed, so queries naming it can match. Option A can only reorder candidates that were retrieved, and the missing sections are not being retrieved at all. Option B adds neighboring text, not the introduction's naming context that lives far away in the document. Option C acts at answer time, after retrieval has already failed.

column2:
You are applying contextual retrieval to 400-page regulatory filings. The contextualization prompt is supposed to include the full source document with each chunk, but the filings are far too large for that, and the per-chunk cost would be prohibitive even where they fit.

How should the context-generation prompt be built for each chunk?

A. Send only the chunk itself and ask Claude to infer the document's context from the chunk's own wording.
B. Send a random sample of 20 chunks from across the filing along with the target chunk to represent the whole.
C. Send the filing's opening chunks plus the chunks immediately preceding the target chunk, omitting the middle of the document.
D. Switch to the largest available model so that the full filing fits in the context window for every chunk.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is the course's strategy for oversized sources: the document's opening chunks usually carry the summary or abstract that explains what the whole document is about, and the chunks just before the target supply its local context, while distant middle sections add little; this keeps each prompt small and cheap. Option A defeats the purpose, since the chunk alone lacks the context being added. Option B supplies unrelated material at random and may omit the introduction entirely. Option D attacks the problem with a bigger context window at far higher cost and does nothing for the per-chunk cost concern.

column2:
Your team adopted contextual retrieval for the claims knowledge base and re-embedded every chunk with its generated context, but left the BM25 index built from the raw chunks. Semantic queries improved, yet keyword queries containing a report code that appears only in the generated context (for example INC-2023-Q4-011) still miss the relevant sections.

What is the cause?

A. BM25 cannot match hyphenated codes such as this one; the tokenizer must be replaced before the added context can help.
B. The contextualized chunk must go into both the vector index and the BM25 index; the lexical index still holds the raw text.
C. The generated context is too short to shift the BM25 term weights; regenerate it with a larger model and longer output.
D. Reciprocal Rank Fusion ignores BM25 results whenever the vector index returns a strong match, so lexical hits are dropped.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: contextual retrieval works by indexing the contextualized chunk (generated context plus original text) in every search path, the vector index and the BM25 index alike. Because the lexical index was left with raw chunks, the report code exists only in the embedded text, so exact-term queries cannot find it. Option A blames tokenization when the term is simply absent from the index. Option C misdiagnoses; a term that is not in the indexed text has no weight regardless of context length. Option D misstates rank fusion, which sums contributions from every list.

column2:
Your document-intake search currently calls the vector index and the BM25 index directly from the request handler, with the merge logic written inline. The team now wants to add a third search method (a title-and-metadata index), and a later proposal calls for a fourth. Each addition currently requires rewriting the handler and its merge code.

Which design best accommodates additional search methods?

A. Chain the methods so that each one searches only within the previous method's results, which eliminates the need for any merge logic.
B. Replace the existing vector and BM25 indexes with the new title-and-metadata index, since it is the most specific of the three.
C. Keep the handler as it is but route the new index's results through the reranker only, bypassing the merge step entirely.
D. Wrap the indexes in a Retriever that requires a common add_document and search interface, fans each query out to every index, and merges the ranked lists.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is the multi-search pipeline design from the course: because every index implements the same small API, a Retriever wrapper can forward add_document and search to each, collect the ranked lists, and merge them with rank fusion, so adding a fourth method means adding one class rather than rewriting the handler. Option A turns parallel, complementary searches into a cascade in which the first method's misses can never be recovered. Option B throws away semantic and lexical coverage. Option C bypasses the merge and gives the new index no influence on which candidates reach the reranker.

column2:
An engineer reports a suspected bug in your hybrid claims search: a section ranked first by the vector index but absent from the BM25 results is consistently outranked in the merged list by a section ranked second in both indexes. The pipeline merges with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, summing 1/(1 + rank) across the indexes.

How should you respond?

A. Explain that this is correct: the section ranked second by both scores 1/3 + 1/3 (about 0.67), the vector-only section scores 1/2; fusion rewards agreement across methods.
B. Confirm the bug: the top vector result should always win, so the vector index's ranks need a higher weight in the merge than the BM25 ranks.
C. Fix the merge so that a section missing from one index receives that index's rank 1 instead of contributing nothing to its score.
D. Replace the fusion step with the raw cosine distance from the vector index so that ties and near-ties are broken numerically.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: under Reciprocal Rank Fusion each index contributes 1/(1 + rank) for the documents it returned and nothing for those it did not, so a section that both methods rank highly accumulates more score than one that only a single method favors; this consensus effect is the intended behavior of hybrid search. Option B would reintroduce the single-method blind spots that hybrid search exists to fix. Option C rewards absence from an index, inverting the meaning of the score. Option D discards the lexical signal entirely and compares quantities that are not on the same scale.

column2:
Your healthcare knowledge base was indexed with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2. A later refactor moved query embedding into a shared service that uses a different embedding model. Retrieval quality collapsed: cosine distances for obviously relevant chunks now cluster near 1.0, and the top results look random.

What is the root cause?

A. The vector index must be rebuilt whenever the query service is redeployed, regardless of which model it uses.
B. Queries must be embedded with the same embedding model that produced the indexed vectors; vectors from different models are not comparable.
C. Titan V2 vectors must be re-normalized on the client before cosine distance is meaningful, and the refactor removed that step.
D. The BM25 index is missing from the new service, so the vector index has no lexical results to fuse with.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: semantic search compares the query embedding with stored chunk embeddings, which only makes sense when both come from the same model, since each model defines its own vector space; embedding queries with a different model produces near-random similarities. Option A invents a coupling that does not exist; the index is model-dependent, not deployment-dependent. Option C is wrong on the facts, since normalization is handled by the embedding API, and it would not explain a collapse that coincided with the model change. Option D concerns lexical search and cannot make correct vector matches disappear.

column2:
Your Bedrock claims extraction prompt scores 9.1 out of 10 on an eval set of 60 synthetic claim letters generated by Claude, yet adjusters report that 15% of real letters, which carry handwritten annotations, scanned tables, and non-standard layouts, yield wrong field values.

How should the eval dataset be rebuilt?

A. Generate 500 synthetic letters instead of 60 and instruct the generator to include unusual layouts, annotations, and scanned tables.
B. Use the pipeline's own production outputs as the expected values so that the eval reflects the real documents it processes.
C. Replace the dataset with a model grader that judges each production output on its own merits, without any expected values.
D. Sample real claim letters from production, have adjusters label the expected value of each field, and store each letter with its expected output as a test case.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: an eval dataset must contain inputs representative of what the prompt sees in production, and for extraction each case needs a trustworthy expected output; sampling real letters and having domain experts label the expected field values provides both. Option A scales up synthetic data that has already proven unrepresentative of production quirks. Option B is circular, since the pipeline's outputs are what is suspected to be wrong. Option C drops ground truth entirely, so the eval could not detect the wrong values that adjusters are reporting.

column2:
Your document-intake eval has 300 labeled test cases, each with the expected policy_number, claim_amount, and date_of_loss. Today a Sonnet model grader reads each output and the expected values and assigns a 1 to 10 score; the grading calls cost more than the extraction itself, and spot checks find the grader awarding 8 out of 10 to outputs with a wrong claim amount.

How should grading be changed for these fields?

A. Keep the model grader but ask it to list strengths and weaknesses before the score so that it grades more strictly and consistently.
B. Switch to human grading for all 300 cases on every run to guarantee that wrong amounts are caught before release.
C. Grade these fields in code by comparing each extracted value with its expected value after normalizing formats; reserve model grading for free-text fields.
D. Raise the grader's temperature so that its scores spread across the full 1 to 10 range instead of clustering near the middle.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: when a test case carries expected values, a code grader can compare each extracted field exactly (after normalizing dates and currency formats), which is deterministic, cheap, and cannot award partial credit to a wrong amount; model graders earn their cost on judgments code cannot make, such as the quality of a free-text summary. Option A improves a model grader's calibration but still applies a subjective judge to an objective comparison. Option B is accurate but far too slow and tedious to run on every iteration. Option D adds randomness to a grader whose problem is leniency, not lack of spread.

column2:
Your Bedrock eval covers 120 varied intake tasks (summaries, coded lists, form-letter drafts). The model grader receives the task, the output, and a single general rubric, and its scores cluster between 6 and 7 regardless of whether the specific task was accomplished; reviewers find that the grader's reasoning rarely mentions task-specific requirements.

What change most improves the grader's ability to separate good outputs from bad ones?

A. Generate solution criteria per test case at dataset-creation time, stating what a good answer to that task must include, and interpolate them into the grader prompt.
B. Ask the grader to output a score only, without any reasoning, so that its scores vary less from run to run and are easier to average across the 120 tasks.
C. Increase the dataset from 120 to 1,200 tasks so that the average score becomes more statistically precise across every task type in the set.
D. Use a larger model as the grader so that it can infer each task's specific requirements on its own from the task text and the output alone.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is the course's dataset exercise: when tasks vary widely, a general rubric cannot tell the grader what success means for each one, so the dataset generator should emit per-case solution criteria alongside the task, and the grader prompt should include them next to the output being judged. Option B removes the reasoning that helps a grader commit to a concrete score and makes middling scores more likely, not less. Option C makes an uninformative signal more precise without making it informative. Option D asks a bigger model to guess requirements that could simply be provided.

column2:
Your team runs a prompt eval on Bedrock after every change to the claims summarization prompt and records only the average score. The last change moved the average from 7.4 to 6.9, and nobody can say which test cases regressed or why, so the change was reverted blindly.

What should each eval run record?

A. Only the per-case scores, since the raw model outputs are too large to keep from run to run and can be regenerated on demand.
B. For each test case: the input, the raw model output, the grader's score, and the grader's reasoning, alongside the aggregate.
C. The aggregate score plus the diff of the prompt between runs, so that future reverts can be made faster and with less guesswork.
D. A single human-written summary of each run so that reports stay readable and the team is not buried in raw output.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: the eval pipeline in the course assembles a result per test case containing the output, the test case, the score, and the grader's reasoning, and it is that per-case record (rendered into a report) that lets engineers see which inputs regressed and what the grader objected to. Option A keeps numbers without the evidence needed to interpret them. Option C explains what changed in the prompt but not how the outputs changed. Option D is unreproducible and depends on someone having already done the analysis the pipeline should enable.

column2:
For complex coverage-dispute analyses in your claims pipeline, evals show that enabling extended thinking is warranted. A developer adds thinking=True and budget_tokens=2048 as keyword arguments to the boto3 converse call, and boto3 rejects the call with a parameter validation error.

How is extended thinking enabled through the Converse API?

A. By passing additionalModelRequestFields={"thinking": {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 2048}} to converse.
B. By adding {"thinking": true} to inferenceConfig alongside temperature and maxTokens.
C. By appending a reasoningContent part to the last user message to request reasoning for that turn.
D. By prefixing the user prompt with a directive to think step by step; there is no API setting for it on Bedrock.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: Converse models the common parameters natively, and model-specific features such as Anthropic's extended thinking are passed through additionalModelRequestFields, where the thinking object enables the feature and sets budget_tokens (which must be at least 1,024). Option B places the setting in inferenceConfig, which accepts only Converse's standard sampling fields. Option C confuses a response part type with a request parameter. Option D is chain-of-thought prompting, a different technique that produces neither the separate reasoning part nor the budget control.

column2:
Your healthcare intake assistant runs with extended thinking and stores conversation history in a database. To save space, the storage layer truncates each reasoningContent part's text to 500 characters. When history is sent back on the next turn, Bedrock rejects the request with an error about the reasoning signature; on other turns the history contains a part holding only redactedContent, which the team planned to drop.

How should reasoning parts be handled when history is resent?

A. Truncate the reasoning text as planned but recompute the signature locally so that it matches the shortened text.
B. Replace each reasoning part with a plain text part containing the same text so that no signature check applies.
C. Store and resend reasoningContent parts exactly as received, including the signature, and pass redactedContent parts through untouched.
D. Drop reasoning and redacted parts from history entirely, since Claude does not need them on later turns.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: the signature on a reasoningContent part is a cryptographic token that lets Claude verify the reasoning text was not modified, so any edit, including truncation, invalidates it; redactedContent is the same reasoning in encrypted form, provided precisely so it can be returned to Claude without losing context. Option A is impossible; the signature is not something your code can generate. Option B strips the signature and presents the reasoning as ordinary assistant text, altering the conversation. Option D discards the context that the redacted form exists to preserve.

column2:
Before launching extended thinking in the intake assistant, QA wants to verify that the response handler copes with a reasoningContent part that contains only redactedContent rather than readable text. In two weeks of testing, no real request has produced a redacted part.

How can the redacted case be exercised deliberately?

A. Set the thinking budget below 1,024 tokens, which causes Bedrock to redact the reasoning instead of returning it.
B. Include the documented magic test string in a user message; Claude then returns redacted reasoning for that request.
C. Send prompts that the safety systems are likely to flag and wait for one whose reasoning comes back redacted.
D. Redacted reasoning cannot be triggered on demand; mock the part shape in unit tests and skip end-to-end coverage.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: Anthropic publishes a special test string that, when included in the user message, guarantees a response whose reasoning part is returned as redactedContent; it exists precisely so applications can test their handling of encrypted reasoning without relying on chance. Option A is wrong, since budgets under 1,024 are rejected, not redacted. Option C is unreliable and inappropriate as a test strategy. Option D gives up a supported end-to-end test in favor of mocks that may not match the real part shape.

column2:
Your claims agent on Bedrock sends a 6,000-token system prompt and 1,200 tokens of tool schemas on every request, with a cachePoint after the system prompt. The usage field shows a full-prefix cacheWriteInputTokens value on every request and cacheReadInputTokens of 0, even for requests two seconds apart. The system prompt begins with a line such as Current time: 2026-08-26T09:14:05Z, refreshed on every request.

Why is the cache never read, and what is the fix?

A. The five-minute cache lifetime is too short for this traffic pattern; increase the request rate so that cache entries never expire.
B. The system prompt exceeds the maximum size for caching; split it into two parts of fewer than 1,024 tokens each with their own cache points.
C. Tool schemas cannot be cached on Bedrock, and their presence in the request invalidates the system prompt's cache entry on every call.
D. The timestamp changes the content before the cache point on every request; move it below the cache point (for example, into the user message).
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: a cache read requires that everything before the cachePoint be identical to a previous request within the cache lifetime; a per-request timestamp at the top of the system prompt guarantees a mismatch, so every request is a fresh write. Moving dynamic content after the cache point preserves the stable prefix. Option A misreads the evidence, since the requests are seconds apart, well inside the lifetime. Option B inverts the rule: 1,024 tokens is the minimum needed to cache, not a maximum. Option C is false; tool definition lists are one of the most common places to put a cache point.

column2:
Your healthcare intake assistant passes a patient-instructions PDF as a document part with citations enabled and renders content[0]["text"] from the response. Clinicians see fluent answers but no source markers, and the compliance team cannot verify which page supports each statement, even though citations were 'turned on'.

What is the correct way to render the response?

A. Iterate over every part in the response content, rendering text parts as answer text and citationsContent parts (cited passage and page) as source markers.
B. Ask Claude in the prompt to append page numbers in brackets after each sentence instead of relying on the citations feature.
C. Enable citations on the user text part as well as the document part, since markers only appear when both parts have it enabled.
D. Increase maxTokens, since citation markers are emitted at the end of the response and are being cut off by the limit.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: with citations enabled, the Converse response interleaves ordinary text parts with citationsContent parts that identify the cited text and where in the document it came from; reading only the first part discards every citation. Option B abandons verifiable citations for model-authored page numbers that cannot be trusted. Option C invents a requirement; citations are enabled on the document part. Option D is wrong on mechanics, since citations are separate parts adjacent to the text they support, not a trailer that gets truncated.

column2:
Your platform team installs Claude Code for engineers who may only use models through your organization's AWS Bedrock account. On first run, Claude Code prompts for an Anthropic API key and, when given one from a personal account, sends every request to Anthropic's API instead of Bedrock.

What configuration makes Claude Code use Bedrock?

A. Add an MCP server to Claude Code that proxies its model requests to the Bedrock endpoint in your organization's account.
B. Paste the Bedrock inference profile ID into the Anthropic API key prompt so that requests are routed to Bedrock instead of Anthropic.
C. Set the CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK environment variable plus the Bedrock region and model settings, so Claude Code calls Bedrock with your AWS credentials.
D. Run init inside a repository that already contains boto3 Bedrock code so that Claude Code detects the provider from the project.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: by default Claude Code targets the Anthropic API, and the course's setup step for Bedrock is to set a small number of environment variables, the Bedrock switch plus region and model configuration, after which Claude Code authenticates with your AWS credentials rather than an Anthropic key. Option A misuses MCP, which adds tools to Claude Code and has nothing to do with which model endpoint it calls. Option B puts a routing identifier where a credential is expected. Option D confuses init, which scans a codebase to write CLAUDE.md, with provider configuration.

column2:
Your team wires a daily GitHub Action in which Claude Code pulls the last 24 hours of CloudWatch errors from the production claims app (deduplicated to a manageable set), diagnoses each, and applies a fix. In the first version the Action commits directly to main and deploys. After two weeks, one automated fix changed a Bedrock model ID to one that is not enabled in production, and it reached users before anyone noticed.

What change most improves the workflow?

A. Have the Action open a pull request with Claude's explanation for each fix, so that a human reviews and merges it.
B. Restrict the Action to errors that recur at least 50 times so that only well-established bugs are ever fixed.
C. Add a second Claude call that reviews the first one's fix and commits it only if the reviewer approves.
D. Limit Claude to files under src/handlers/ so that configuration changes such as model IDs are impossible.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is the course's workflow: the agent should explain and propose fixes through a pull request that a human reviews before merge; automated debugging still requires human review of proposed changes, and a PR preserves the speed of automated diagnosis while keeping a person accountable for what ships. Option B changes which errors get attention, not whether a bad fix can deploy. Option C substitutes one model's judgment for another's on a change with production impact, without human accountability. Option D is a brittle path restriction that would also block legitimate fixes, and many bad fixes live inside handler code anyway.

column2:
Your company wants to build its first autonomous agent on Bedrock. Three candidates are proposed: (1) an agent that writes and runs unit tests for the claims codebase and opens PRs; (2) an agent that approves and issues claim payments up to $50,000 without review; (3) an agent that answers rare, low-value FAQ lookups. Each would loop over a small, focused toolset and inspect its environment through tool calls.

Which candidate best matches the qualities of a good first agent, and why?

A. Candidate 2, because the highest-value task justifies the investment in an agent, its tooling, and its evaluation suite.
B. Candidate 3, because a low-stakes task is the safest possible place to learn how agents behave in production before scaling up.
C. Candidate 2, provided the agent reports a confidence score and any payment below 0.8 confidence is held for review.
D. Candidate 1, because the work is high value while a mistaken edit is cheap to catch in review and tests, with no direct economic or safety impact.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: the course's analysis of Claude Code and Computer Use concludes that agents suit high-value tasks where failures do not cause large economic or safety damage; writing code is valuable, and a bad change is recoverable through review and tests. Option A picks value while ignoring the unbounded cost of an autonomous payment error. Option B is safe but so low in value that the effort of building and evaluating an agent is not justified. Option C tries to make the risky candidate acceptable with a self-reported confidence gate, which is not a reliable control.
